summary: C.R.E.W is a pixel-style simulation, strategy and story game where students design, launch and operate an Earth-observation CubeSat over Sarawak's Rajang River. As Lead Systems Engineer, the player works across four departments (Planning, Engineering, Communications and Science) to choose objectives, lock requirements, build the satellite, pick a launch and orbit, then run the mission in accelerated time. A dashboard shows six limits at all times: budget, mass, power, communications, data and lifetime, so a change in one subsystem shows its effect on the others. Advisors give hints but never take control. Each run ends with a score and a debrief that explains why the result happened. Missions last 10 to 20 minutes, so one fits a lesson. It turns the abstract trade-offs of real mission design into hands-on decisions for students aged 13 to 17 with no prior knowledge, and links Earth observation to local issues such as flooding, sediment and land-use change. Built in godot 4(exported WebGL) for the web and grounded in NASA's CubeSat 101.
details:
C.R.E.W.

A browser STEM game where Sarawak students design, test, launch and fly their own CubeSat.

From Sarawak to space. Give curiosity a mission.

1. What it does and how it works

C.R.E.W. is a free browser game for secondary-school students in Sarawak, roughly ages 13 to 17. Players join a fictional Sarawak space academy and run a complete small-satellite mission. They design a real-format 3U CubeSat, which is three 10 cm cubes stacked together. Its job is to observe the Rajang River and Sarawak's forests. Players then prove the satellite is ready, launch it, fly it and learn from the results.

The game follows the loop real engineers use: problem → objective → build → test → redesign → launch → operate → downlink → debrief → improve.

1. Crew and briefing. Players meet a crew of student specialists, such as a camera lead and a radio lead, in a walk-around mission station. They choose a science objective and a priority zone, and the game turns that choice into measurable requirements.

2. Workshop. Players drag parts into a pixel-art cut-away of the satellite: cameras, reaction wheels, radios, solar wings and batteries. Live readouts track mass, volume, power, battery, storage, data link and budget. Overpacking fails the design checks for clear reasons, for example "the dispenser door can't close". Players then redesign until the satellite passes.

3. Launch and ground planning. Players compare three rideshare launches and three ground stations. The numbers come from the game's orbit model: passes, local time, cloud cover, contact time and orbital lifetime.

4. Test lab. Seven animated readiness tests (T1–T7) cover fit, mass, battery, a day-in-the-life power run, vibration and thermal-vacuum, communications, and space-debris rules. Changing the hardware cancels earlier passes, so players have to re-test. A seven-station GO/NO-GO poll must be earned.

5. Launch and operations. A launch cinematic shows the player's own satellite design. Players then lock onto the first signal over Kuching by tuning out the Doppler shift, and decide what to capture and downlink during a simulated 10-day campaign. Problems come up along the way: eclipse power shortfalls, downlink bottlenecks and a storm over Kuching.

6. Debrief. The mission is rated success, partial success or failure based on the usable data returned. The debrief explains why, gives engineering recommendations and offers ways to retry.

It needs no install, no login and no server, and it runs in English and Bahasa Melayu.

2. Benefits

• Real engineering thinking, not trivia. Students learn trade-offs, budgets, testing and iteration by doing them. Failure is part of the lesson, not a game-over screen.

• Local relevance. The mission looks at Sarawak's own river, forests and towns, and ties STEM to places students know.

• Accessible. It runs in any modern browser and works offline after loading. It has no cost, no accounts, two languages, and options for reduced motion, high contrast and instant text.

• Classroom-ready. It includes a Teacher View with a CSV export of results, an optional before-and-after quiz, badges, a "Science & Sources" page, and a Judge Demo mode that starts from a ready-built satellite.

3. Intended impact

Sarawak plans to set up its own space agency and is targeting its first CubeSat launch by 2030. However, only about 13% of Form 4–5 science-stream students reportedly take STEM Package A. C.R.E.W. aims to close that gap. It gives students their first mission before they choose their subjects, so that "space engineer" feels like a real, local career path. The goal is more students choosing STEM and Sarawak's future satellite workforce growing at home.

Sources: Borneo Post, 20 May 2026 (Space Agency and 2030 launch target); Dr Annuar Rapaee, Borneo Post, 14 October 2025 (about 13% STEM Package A participation).

Our message: from Sarawak to space. Give curiosity a mission.

4. Tools, languages, hardware and software

• Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS

• Game and interface: React 19 for the screens, Phaser 4 for the 2D game scenes (sky, hangar, launch, orbit), GSAP for animation, Zustand for game state, Tailwind CSS

• Science model: a separate TypeScript simulation, kept apart from the game engine, covering orbit, power, design rules, testing, operations, observations and scoring

• Maps: real Natural Earth coastlines via world-atlas and topojson-client

• Saving: browser storage (IndexedDB, with a localStorage fallback) and three save slots

• Build and testing: Vite, Vitest (science and state tests), Playwright (end-to-end mission test)

• Hosting: Vercel, live at https://crew-landing-psi.vercel.app/

• Reference: NASA CubeSat 101 (2017), used for the mission process: dispensers, margins, testing, power runs, readiness reviews and debris rules

• Pitch video: HyperFrames (HTML to video), Three.js (3D Earth and CubeSat), VoiceStudio text-to-speech, an original music score written in Python, CC0 sound effects, and FFmpeg. Gameplay was recorded from the live game in Chrome.

• Hardware: a standard Windows laptop. The game needs no special hardware.

5. How it is creative

• Failure is the teacher. The overpacked satellite is designed to fail. The fix-and-pass moment is the payoff, which mirrors how real missions work.

• Your design really matters. The launch cinematic, tests and results all use the satellite the player built, not a scripted one.

• Hands-on space operations. Tuning out the Doppler shift to catch the first signal over Kuching turns radio physics into a skill-based mini-game.

• Honest debriefs. The game explains why a mission partly succeeded, such as data that was never downlinked, and how to do better.

• Local storytelling. Sarawak characters, places and problems sit inside a premium pixel-art and mission-control look.

6. Factors our team considered

• Audience: reading level, ages 13–17, two languages, and short sessions that fit a class period.

• Accuracy versus fun: the physics is simplified, and the game says so plainly. The academy, launches, stations, prices and part ratings are marked as fictional assumptions. NASA guidance is cited for process only, never for invented numbers.

• Access and equity: free, no login, works offline, runs on modest school computers, and includes accessibility settings.

• Privacy: no accounts, no backend, and student data stays on the device.

• Teachers: a Teacher View, export, a quiz, and a judge or demo shortcut.

• Quality: automated science and end-to-end tests, a QA report, and a source register.

• Local fit: a Sarawak setting and real geography, connected to the state's 2030 space goal.
